content_voiceover: This is flagged as a must test topic, the I P S S Molecular model, or I P S S M, from Papaemmanuil and colleagues in N E J M Evidence. It builds on clinical variables, bone marrow blasts, platelets, hemoglobin, and cytogenetic risk category, then adds molecular data from sixteen genes. The table ranks each gene's adjusted hazard ratio and model weight. The heaviest hitters, with hazard ratios above two, are T P 53 multi hit, M L L P T D, and F L T 3 with I T D or T K D mutations, these carry the most prognostic weight and push patients toward higher risk categories. A second tier of moderately weighted genes includes S F 3 B 1 with the 5 q signature, N P M 1, R U N X 1, N RAS, E T V 6, I D H 2, C B L, E Z H 2, U 2 A F 1, S R S F 2, D N M T 3 A, A S X L 1, and K RAS. Beyond these seventeen named variables, there's a residual term capturing fifteen additional minor genes, so more than ninety percent of patients end up with at least one detectable molecular abnormality feeding into this score.
keypoints: IPSS-M combines clinical, cytogenetic, and 16-gene molecular data
Top weighted adverse genes: TP53 multi-hit, MLL-PTD, FLT3
Second tier genes include SF3B1, NPM1, RUNX1, NRAS, IDH2, ASXL1, and more
A residual term covers 15 additional minor genes
Marked as high yield, expect direct exam questions on this model
keypoint_voiceover: This slide is explicitly flagged high yield, so memorize the top three genes, T P 53 multi hit, M L L P T D, and F L T 3, as the strongest adverse predictors in I P S S M, and know that the model layers clinical data plus cytogenetics plus a panel of sixteen named genes plus a residual term for minor genes.
